analysis.one_liner: Criminalizes posting nonconsensual intimate images, including AI fakes, and requires websites to remove them within 48 hours.
analysis.headline: The bill became law: the Senate passed it unanimously on February 13, 2025, the House passed it 409-2 on April 28, and the President signed it on May 19, 2025 (Public Law 119-12).
analysis.plain_summary: The TAKE IT DOWN Act makes it a federal crime to knowingly post intimate images of someone without their consent, including AI-generated 'deepfakes' that look real, or to threaten to post them. Violators face up to 2-3 years in prison, fines, restitution, and forfeiture of proceeds. It also requires websites that host user-generated content to set up a removal process and take down flagged intimate images within 48 hours of a valid request, with the Federal Trade Commission enforcing that duty.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of 'revenge porn' and AI-generated fake intimate images, most often women and teenagers, gain a federal criminal penalty against publishers and threats, plus a guaranteed fast way to get images pulled down from major websites. Parents of minors get the same protections, and victims can recover restitution for psychological, financial, or reputational harm.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime to knowingly publish authentic intimate images of an adult without consent where the person had a reasonable expectation of privacy and the publication causes or is intended to cause harm, punishable by up to 2 years in prison [S4].

Covers 'digital forgeries' — AI-generated or altered intimate images of an identifiable person that are indistinguishable from real ones — closing a gap that left deepfake victims with little recourse [S4].
Criminalizes threats to publish such images for intimidation, coercion, extortion, or to cause mental distress, targeting sextortion of teens and adults [S4].

Requires covered platforms — public websites and apps that primarily host user-generated content — to set up a notice-and-removal process and remove flagged images within 48 hours, with the FTC enforcing compliance [S4].
Courts must order restitution to victims and forfeiture of proceeds from violations [S4].

analysis.who_pays: People who publish or threaten to publish nonconsensual intimate images face prison, fines, restitution, and forfeiture. Covered platforms — social media sites, forums, and apps — bear the cost of building and operating a 48-hour takedown system, though the bill shields them from lawsuits for good-faith removals.

drawbacks.text: A notice-and-takedown system with a 48-hour deadline and a liability shield for good-faith removals gives platforms an incentive to take down flagged material first and ask questions later, which free-speech advocates warn can sweep up lawful, consensual, or newsworthy content [S4].

The law turns on whether a publication 'causes harm' and whether content is 'a matter of public concern' — terms that leave room for argument about satire, art, news reporting, and public-figure cases [S4].
Enforcement of the takedown duty runs through the FTC, so victims cannot directly sue a platform that ignores a removal request; they rely on agency action [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections address a real and growing harm — nonconsensual intimate images and AI deepfakes — with meaningful criminal penalties and a concrete takedown deadline. The main cost is the risk that fast, shielded takedowns sweep up some lawful speech, a trade-off speech advocates flagged; the law's exceptions for public-concern content, law enforcement, medical and legal uses, and self-publication are designed to limit that, but how narrowly they are applied will determine whether the trade-off is worth it.

outcome.mechanism: It swept through Congress — passed by the Senate unanimously on February 13, 2025, by the House 409-2 on April 28 — and the President signed it on May 19, 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Ted Cruz introduced S. 146 in the Senate on January 16, 2025, and it drew 21 cosponsors split between the parties (11 of 45 Senate Democrats and 10 of 55 Senate Republicans) [S1] [S5].
The Senate Commerce Committee was discharged from the bill by unanimous consent on February 13, 2025, and the Senate passed it the same day without amendment by unanimous consent [S6].

The House took it up on April 28, 2025 under a fast-track procedure requiring a two-thirds vote, and passed it 409-2, with 202 of 213 voting House Democrats and 207 of 220 voting House Republicans in favor [S6] [S7].
The President signed it on May 19, 2025, and it became Public Law 119-12 [S3] [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Victims of nonconsensual intimate imagery, including deepfake victims, gained a federal criminal remedy and a guaranteed 48-hour takedown right. No concentrated interest defeated the bill, so the usual losing side here is limited to platforms bearing compliance costs and publishers facing new criminal penalties.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly bipartisan: every voting Senate member allowed it to pass by unanimous consent, and the House vote was 409-2, with both parties nearly unanimous (202-0 among voting Democrats, 207-2 among voting Republicans).

industries.industry: Social media and user-generated content platforms
industries.note: Platforms must build a removal process, publicize it, and take down flagged images within 48 hours, which imposes real compliance costs. But they also gain a liability shield for good-faith removals, and their incentive to clear flagged content quickly rather than carefully is the main free-speech concern with the law.

The law criminalizes publishing AI-generated intimate images of identifiable people, so creators and distributors of such material face up to 2 years in prison and forfeiture of proceeds. People who use AI tools to make realistic fakes of real individuals lose a legal gray area they previously operated in.
